hypotheses.title: LsdApi3OracleReader setters lack onlyGovernor modifier
hypotheses.description: The functions setDataFeedIds, setQuoteTokens, and setMaxStaleTimes in LsdApi3OracleReader are declared external but have no access control modifier, unlike the equivalent functions in Api3OracleReader and PythOracleReader which are guarded by onlyGovernor. Any external caller can overwrite the dataFeedId, quoteToken, and maxStaleTime for any token, directly controlling the price returned by getPrice_e36.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls setDataFeedIds([victimToken], [attackerChosenFeedId]) to point the token at a feed they control or a manipulated feed. 2) Attacker calls setQuoteTokens to set an arbitrary quote token. 3) Attacker calls setMaxStaleTimes to set a huge stale time. 4) The oracle now returns an attacker-controlled price, which is consumed by InitOracle/InitCore for collateral valuation and liquidation.
hypotheses.impact: Full manipulation of collateral and debt valuation for any token using this oracle, enabling under-collateralized borrowing, theft via liquidation, and protocol insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add the onlyGovernor modifier to setDataFeedIds, setQuoteTokens, and setMaxStaleTimes.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.updateOrder missing ownership check on order
hypotheses.description: updateOrder verifies that initPosIds[msg.sender][_posId] != 0 and that the order is Active, but never checks that order.initPosId equals the caller's initPosId. Any caller who owns any position can update any other user's active order by passing their own _posId (to satisfy the position check) while supplying an arbitrary _orderId belonging to a different position. The order's triggerPrice, limitPrice, collAmt, and tokenOut are overwritten.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates their own position to obtain a valid _posId. 2) Attacker calls updateOrder(attackerPosId, victimOrderId, maliciousTrigger, maliciousTokenOut, maliciousLimit, maliciousCollAmt). 3) The victim's order is rewritten; when fillOrder is later called, the victim's collateral is sold at the attacker's chosen prices/tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Victim's stop-loss/take-profit orders are hijacked, causing them to be filled at manipulated prices and tokens, resulting in loss of collateral and debt repayment on unfavorable terms.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `_require(order.initPosId == initPosId, Errors.INVALID_INPUT);` in updateOrder before mutating the order.

hypotheses.title: MoeSwapHelper uses amountOutMin=0 for exact-in swaps
hypotheses.description: For `SwapType.OpenExactIn` and `SwapType.CloseExactIn`, the helper calls `swapExactTokensForTokens(balance, 0, path, ...)` with `amountOutMin = 0`. The caller (`MarginTradingHook.coreCallback`) only checks `amtOut` for `CloseExactOut`; for exact-in swaps there is no minimum-out enforcement anywhere in the path. A malicious router/pair or a sandwich attacker can drain nearly all value from the swap.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker observes a victim's `openPos`/`reducePos`/`fillOrder` transaction that routes through `MoeSwapHelper`, front-runs the pool to move the price, and lets the swap execute at a terrible rate. The hook accepts whatever `amtOut` results because no min-out is enforced for exact-in.
hypotheses.impact: Direct loss of user funds on every exact-in swap; the position is opened/reduced at an arbitrarily bad price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Pass a real `amountOutMin` derived from `_swapInfo` (add a min-out field) and enforce it in the helper, or have `coreCallback` compute and check a minimum for exact-in swaps.

hypotheses.title: removeCollateral transfers tokens out before health check
hypotheses.description: removeCollateral() decollateralizes, burns to underlying, and transfers the full collateral balance to msg.sender via _transmitTokenOut, and only afterwards calls getPosHealthCurrent_e18 to compute health. There is no minHealth parameter and no revert if the resulting position is unhealthy. A user can therefore remove all collateral from a position, leaving debt unpaid and the position underwater.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker opens a leveraged position. 2) Attacker calls removeCollateral with _shares equal to the full collateral. 3) The function decollateralizes and transfers all underlying to the attacker. 4) The health check at the end only returns the value; it does not revert. 5) Attacker walks away with collateral while debt remains, leaving the protocol with bad debt.
hypotheses.impact: Direct loss of protocol funds via bad debt; the position owner can drain collateral without repaying debt.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require the post-removal health to be >= 1e18 (or a caller-supplied minimum) before transferring tokens out, or perform the health check before the transfer.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.initialize callable by anyone to set swapHelper
hypotheses.description: MarginTradingHook.initialize(address _swapHelper) is external and only guarded by the initializer modifier, with no access control. If the proxy is deployed without atomically calling initialize in the constructor (or if initialization is front-run), any external actor can call initialize first and set swapHelper to an arbitrary contract. The swapHelper is invoked in coreCallback to perform swaps for every open/increase/reduce position.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes the proxy deployment or front-runs the legitimate initialize call. 2) Attacker calls initialize(attackerControlledSwapHelper). 3) Attacker's swap helper is now used in coreCallback for all users' swaps, allowing it to steal tokens or return manipulated amounts.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of user funds during swaps, manipulation of position collateral, and potential draining of tokens held by the hook during operations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict initialize to a trusted deployer/governor (e.g., onlyGovernor) or ensure atomic initialization in the proxy constructor.

hypotheses.title: PythOracleReader accepts negative prices via int64->uint cast
hypotheses.description: `int(price).toUint256()` is called on the raw Pyth price without checking that `price > 0`. Pyth can return negative or zero prices (e.g., during extreme market events or for misconfigured feeds). A negative int64 cast to uint256 wraps to a huge value, and a zero price yields zero, both of which corrupt health/credit calculations downstream.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker waits for (or triggers via a thin market) a Pyth update where the price is negative or zero, then calls any function that reads `getPrice_e36` (e.g., `InitCore.liquidate`, `getPosHealthCurrent_e18`, `MarginTradingHook.fillOrder`). The wrapped huge price inflates collateral credit or deflates debt, letting the attacker liquidate healthy positions or borrow against inflated collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong accounting, unfair liquidations, potential protocol insolvency from over-borrowing against a wrapped price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `_require(price > 0, Errors.ZERO_VALUE)` (or a dedicated error) before casting, and reject non-positive prices.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.updateOrder does not validate _tokenOut
hypotheses.description: `_createOrder` enforces `_tokenOut == marginPos.baseAsset || _tokenOut == marginPos.quoteAsset`, but `updateOrder` omits this check and blindly writes `order.tokenOut = _tokenOut`. A user can set `tokenOut` to an arbitrary token, and `fillOrder` will then `safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, order.recipient, amtOut)` of that arbitrary token from the filler.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker creates a position, adds an order, then calls `updateOrder` with `_tokenOut` set to an arbitrary valuable token (e.g., USDC) that the filler holds. When a filler calls `fillOrder`, the hook pulls `amtOut` of the attacker-chosen token from the filler and sends it to the attacker (the order recipient), while the attacker only pays the borrow-token repayment.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of arbitrary ERC20 tokens from any filler who calls `fillOrder` on the malicious order.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `updateOrder`, re-apply the same `_tokenOut == baseAsset || _tokenOut == quoteAsset` check used in `_createOrder`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder reads order into memory then writes status after external calls
hypotheses.description: fillOrder() loads the Order into memory, performs multiple external calls (safeTransferFrom on borrToken and order.tokenOut, IInitCore.repay, IInitCore.decollateralize) and only afterwards sets __orders[_orderId].status = Filled. Because the status check `order.status == OrderStatus.Active` is performed on the memory copy, any reentrant call into fillOrder() during the external calls will still see the on-chain status as Active and pass the check, allowing the same order to be filled multiple times.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious ERC20 as order.tokenOut (or uses a token with a transfer hook) and gets a victim to create an order with that tokenOut. 2) Attacker calls fillOrder(orderId). 3) During IERC20(order.tokenOut).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, order.recipient, amtOut), the malicious token reenters fillOrder(orderId). 4) The reentrant call re-reads __orders[_orderId] which is still Active, passes validation, and executes repay/decollateralize again. 5) Repeat until the position's collateral is drained.
hypotheses.impact: The same order can be filled repeatedly, draining the position's collateral and repaying debt with the attacker's tokens multiple times, causing loss of funds to the position owner and potentially leaving bad debt in the protocol.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set __orders[_orderId].status = OrderStatus.Filled (or a non-reentrant guard) before any external call, and re-read the order from storage after external calls.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder transfers tokens to recipient before repaying/decollateralizing
hypotheses.description: In fillOrder(), the executor's borrToken is pulled in and then order.tokenOut is transferred to order.recipient before IInitCore.repay and IInitCore.decollateralize are executed. If order.tokenOut is a token with a transfer hook (ERC777/ERC1155-like), the recipient can reenter fillOrder or other hook functions while the order is still Active and the position's debt/collateral have not yet been updated.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates an order where tokenOut is a malicious token with a transfer callback. 2) Attacker (as filler) calls fillOrder. 3) During safeTransferFrom of tokenOut to recipient, the recipient contract reenters fillOrder with the same orderId. 4) The reentrant call sees status Active and repeats the flow, pulling more borrToken from the filler and transferring more tokenOut, while repay/decollateralize from the first call have not yet executed.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of the order; the position's collateral can be decollateralized multiple times, and the filler can be drained of borrToken.
hypotheses.recommendation: Mark the order as Filled before any external transfer, and use a reentrancy guard on fillOrder.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.fillOrder lacks trigger price re-validation and order owner consent
hypotheses.description: fillOrder validates the trigger price condition via _validateTriggerPrice, but the order's recipient is set at creation to msg.sender (the position owner). The function transfers order.tokenOut from the filler to order.recipient and repays debt, then decollateralizes to msg.sender (the filler). This is by design, but combined with the updateOrder vulnerability (no ownership check), an attacker can rewrite a victim's order to set tokenOut to a worthless token and collAmt to the full collateral, then fill it themselves to drain the victim's collateral.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker exploits updateOrder to set victim's order.tokenOut to a worthless token and collAmt to max. 2) Attacker calls fillOrder(victimOrderId). 3) Attacker repays a small debt amount and receives the victim's full collateral via decollateralize to msg.sender, while the victim receives worthless tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Complete drain of victim's collateral from their margin position.
hypotheses.recommendation: Fix updateOrder ownership check; additionally consider restricting fillOrder to only fill orders whose tokenOut is a valid base/quote asset (already checked at creation but not re-checked on update).

hypotheses.title: liquidate bypasses health check for underwater positions, allowing bad debt
hypotheses.description: In `liquidate`, the post-liquidation health check is skipped when `vars.health_e18 == 0` ("bypass this for underwater position"). `getPosHealthCurrent_e18` returns 0 only when `borrowCredit_e36 > 0` and `collateralCredit_e36 == 0`, i.e. the position has debt but no collateral credit. A liquidator can repay a tiny `_repayShares` and receive `shares = min(computed, collAmt)` of collateral, but the remaining debt is never checked. If the position has collateral with zero credit (e.g. collFactor 0 or price 0), the liquidator can extract collateral while leaving the debt unpaid.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker finds a position with `health_e18 == 0` (debt > 0, collateral credit == 0). 2) Attacker calls `liquidate` with `_repayShares = 1` and `_poolOut` = the collateral pool. 3) `_ensurePosHealthAfterLiq` is skipped, so the position remains with debt and no collateral. 4) Attacker receives collateral shares for a trivial repayment.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol accrues bad debt; remaining lenders in the pool cannot be repaid; collateral is extracted for near-zero cost.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the `if (vars.health_e18 != 0)` bypass, or require that after liquidation the position's debt is fully repaid when collateral credit is zero.

hypotheses.title: InitCore.callback allows arbitrary external callback target
hypotheses.description: InitCore.callback(address _to, uint _value, bytes _data) is public and only checks that _to != address(this). It then calls ICallbackReceiver(_to).coreCallback{value: _value}(msg.sender, _data). Any external caller can invoke callback with an arbitrary _to contract, causing InitCore to make an external call to an attacker-controlled contract with attacker-supplied data and value. The callback receiver sees msg.sender == CORE (InitCore), which may be trusted by other contracts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious contract implementing coreCallback. 2) Attacker calls InitCore.callback(attackerContract, 0, maliciousData). 3) InitCore calls attackerContract.coreCallback with msg.sender == InitCore. 4) If any protocol contract trusts calls originating from InitCore (e.g., MarginTradingHook.coreCallback checks msg.sender == CORE and _sender == address(this)), the attacker can potentially trigger privileged paths.
hypotheses.impact: Potential unauthorized invocation of callback receivers that trust InitCore as caller, leading to unauthorized state changes or fund movements in dependent contracts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict callback to be callable only internally (e.g., during multicall) or add an authorization check that the caller is a legitimate position owner / the multicall context.

hypotheses.title: LendingPool.mint uses stale cash snapshot allowing share inflation via direct donation
hypotheses.description: `mint` computes `amt = newCash - _cash` where `_cash` is the stored `cash` variable, but `newCash` is the live token balance. If an attacker transfers underlying tokens directly to the pool (donation) before a mint, `newCash - _cash` includes the donated amount, so the minter receives shares for tokens they did not supply. Because `cash` is only updated to `newCash` after minting, the donated tokens are effectively credited to the minter's shares, diluting existing suppliers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker transfers X underlying tokens directly to the LendingPool (no mint call). 2) Attacker (or victim) triggers any mint path (e.g. via MoneyMarketHook deposit or MarginTradingHook). 3) `newCash - _cash` includes X, so shares are minted for X even though the minter only supplied their own amount. 4) Attacker redeems shares to extract the donated value plus a share of others' deposits.
hypotheses.impact: Direct theft of pool assets; existing suppliers' share value is diluted; pool accounting drifts from real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track deposits via an internal accounting variable updated only on mint/burn/borrow/repay, or compute `amt` from the actual transfer amount passed by the caller rather than balance delta.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.fillOrder lacks slippage protection for filler
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` computes `amtOut` and `repayAmt` from the order's `limitPrice_e36` and current pool state, then transfers `repayAmt` of borrow token from the filler and `amtOut` of `tokenOut` to the recipient. There is no `minAmtOut`/`maxRepayAmt` parameter, so the filler cannot bound the trade. Between submission and inclusion, interest accrual or a collateral change can shift `repayAmt`/`amtOut` against the filler.
hypotheses.attackPath: An order owner (or anyone who can influence the position, e.g., via a pending `increasePos`/`repayDebt` in the same block) can cause `_calculateRepaySize`/`_calculateFillOrderInfo` to return values unfavorable to the filler. The filler's transaction still succeeds because no min/max is checked, extracting value from the filler.
hypotheses.impact: Filler loses funds on every fill where the computed amounts drift; griefing vector against keepers/liquidators.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `_minAmtOut` and `_maxRepayAmt` parameters to `fillOrder` and enforce them before transferring tokens.

hypotheses.title: coreCallback trusts swapHelper to return funds; no reentrancy guard on hook
hypotheses.description: coreCallback() transfers the entire tokenIn balance to swapHelper and then reads the resulting tokenOut balance, assuming the helper swapped correctly. The hook has no reentrancy guard, and swapHelper is a mutable storage address set at initialize. If swapHelper is a malicious/compromised contract (or if a token with a callback is used), it can reenter the hook's public functions (openPos/increasePos/reducePos/removeCollateral) while the multicall is mid-flight, before health checks and state updates complete.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker controls a token used as tokenIn/tokenOut (or the swapHelper is set to an attacker contract via governance compromise — but even without that, a token with ERC777-style hooks can reenter). 2) During coreCallback, the token transfer to swapHelper triggers a hook. 3) The hook reenters removeCollateral or reducePos on the same position while the multicall's health check has not yet run. 4) Attacker extracts collateral before the position is validated as healthy.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral can be withdrawn while the position is temporarily unhealthy, leaving bad debt; or funds can be siphoned via reentrant calls that bypass the intended health/slippage checks.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a nonReentrant guard to MarginTradingHook's external entry points and coreCallback, and validate swapHelper output amounts against expected minimums inside coreCallback.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.updateOrder allows changing tokenOut to arbitrary asset
hypotheses.description: `updateOrder` overwrites `order.tokenOut` with `_tokenOut` without re-validating that `_tokenOut` is `baseAsset` or `quoteAsset` of the margin position (unlike `_createOrder` which does check). An owner (or anyone who can call `updateOrder` on their own order) can set `tokenOut` to an arbitrary token, and `fillOrder` will then attempt `IERC20(order.tokenOut).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, order.recipient, amtOut)` and `decollateralize` to `msg.sender`. If `tokenOut` is not the collateral token, the accounting in `_calculateFillOrderInfo` uses the wrong branch, and the executor may receive collateral while paying a worthless token.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a position and an order. 2) Calls `updateOrder` with `_tokenOut` set to an attacker-controlled token. 3) Calls `fillOrder`; the branch logic mis-computes `amtOut` and the attacker receives collateral for a worthless `tokenOut` payment.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of position collateral / incorrect accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `updateOrder`, re-validate `_tokenOut == marginPos.baseAsset || _tokenOut == marginPos.quoteAsset`.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder lets executor drain collateral without repaying full debt
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` computes `repayShares`/`repayAmt` from `_calculateRepaySize`, which scales the debt proportionally to `order.collAmt / totalCollAmt`. The executor pays `repayAmt` of borrow token and receives `order.collAmt` of collateral, but the position's remaining debt is not re-checked for health after the fill. Because `_calculateFillOrderInfo` rounds `amtOut` in favor of the order owner while `repayAmt` is computed with `debtShareToAmtCurrent` (rounding up), the executor can pick `_collAmt` values where the collateral removed is worth more than the debt repaid at the limit price, leaving the position under-collateralized.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes an active stop-loss/take-profit order. 2) Attacker calls `fillOrder` with the order's `collAmt` chosen so that `collTokenAmt - repayAmt*limit` is maximized (e.g. when `limitPrice` is favorable vs mark price). 3) Attacker receives `amtOut` of `tokenOut` and the position's collateral is reduced by `order.collAmt` while only `repayShares` of debt is repaid. 4) The remaining position is now unhealthy; attacker repeats or leaves bad debt for the protocol.
hypotheses.impact: Position becomes under-collateralized / bad debt accrues to the lending pool; order owner's collateral is sold below fair value.
hypotheses.recommendation: After `fillOrder`, call `_validateHealth` on the position (or require health >= 1e18) and cap `amtOut` so the executor cannot extract more value than the debt repaid at the mark price.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder transfers tokens before verifying order owner's collateral
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` reads `order.collAmt` and computes `amtOut`/`repayAmt` from the order snapshot, but the position's collateral may have changed since the order was created (e.g. via `removeCollateral`, `reducePos`, or another `fillOrder`). The function only checks `getCollAmt != 0` and then calls `decollateralize(order.initPosId, marginPos.collPool, order.collAmt, msg.sender)` — if the position no longer holds `order.collAmt` shares, `decollateralize` will revert or, worse, the executor already paid `repayAmt` and received `amtOut` before the decollateralize call. The order status is only set to Filled after all transfers, so a partially-executed order can leave the executor with tokens but no collateral.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates a position and a stop-loss/take-profit order with `collAmt = X`. 2) Attacker (or another party) reduces the position's collateral via `removeCollateral`/`reducePos` so the position holds less than X. 3) Attacker calls `fillOrder` when the trigger price is met; the function transfers `repayAmt` from attacker to the hook and `amtOut` from attacker to `order.recipient`, then calls `decollateralize` which reverts or transfers less than expected. 4) Attacker can also front-run a legitimate filler by draining collateral first, causing the filler's tx to revert after they've already approved/transferred.
hypotheses.impact: Executors can lose the repay tokens they transferred in (if the subsequent decollateralize reverts, the whole tx reverts, but if it succeeds with less collateral the accounting is wrong); order owners can be griefed; position accounting becomes inconsistent with order state.
hypotheses.recommendation: Re-validate `order.collAmt <= getCollAmt(...)` inside `fillOrder` before any token transfers, and update order status to Filled before external calls (or use a reentrancy-safe pattern).

hypotheses.title: LendingPool.burn uses stale cash and can over-redeem after donation
hypotheses.description: `burn` computes `amt = _toAmt(sharesToBurn, _cash + totalDebt, totalSupply())` using the stored `cash` rather than the live balance. If tokens were donated to the pool, `totalAssets()` (live) exceeds `_cash + totalDebt`, so the redeemer receives less than the fair share; conversely if `cash` is stale-high relative to actual balance, `amt <= _cash` check may pass while the pool lacks tokens, causing transfer revert or draining other accounting. The mismatch between stored `cash` and real balance is the root cause.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker donates tokens to inflate real balance without updating `cash`. 2) A redeemer burns shares; `_toAmt` uses stale `_cash`, so the redeemer is underpaid and the surplus remains in the pool. 3) Attacker later mints to capture the surplus via the mint path above, or drains via repeated cycles.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong redemption amounts; value leakage between users; pool accounting diverges from real holdings.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use live `IERC20(underlyingToken).balanceOf(address(this))` for `_totalAssets` in burn, or forbid direct donations by tracking internal cash strictly.

hypotheses.title: WLpMoeMasterChef.getPendingRewards divides by lpSupply without zero check
hypotheses.description: `getPendingRewards` computes `moeRewards[0] * ONE_E18 / lpSupply` and `extraRewards[0] * ONE_E18 / lpSupply` where `lpSupply = IMasterChef(MASTER_CHEF).getDeposit(pid, address(this))`. If the contract's deposit for that pid is zero (e.g. all wLp for that pid have been unwrapped, or the pid was never deposited), this reverts with division by zero, bricking the view function. More critically, `_transferRewards` uses `pidAccRewardPerShares_e18` which is only updated in `updateRewards` when `lpSupply != 0`; if lpSupply is zero at update time, rewards accrued are silently skipped and later distributed to remaining holders, mis-accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker unwraps all wLp for a pid, making `lpSupply == 0`. 2) Any call to `getPendingRewards` for that pid reverts. 3) If new deposits occur later, `updateRewards` skips the accrual branch, so rewards earned while supply was zero are lost or misallocated.
hypotheses.impact: DoS on view function; reward accounting drift; rewards lost or misallocated among holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard `lpSupply == 0` by returning zero pending rewards, and ensure `updateRewards` still records accrued rewards even when supply is zero (or explicitly skip and document).

hypotheses.title: LsdApi3OracleReader missing block.timestamp > timestamp guard
hypotheses.description: Unlike `Api3OracleReader.getPrice_e36`, this function computes `block.timestamp - timestamp` without first checking `block.timestamp > timestamp`. If the API3 feed returns a future timestamp (clock skew, malicious/compromised feed, or a chain reorg), the subtraction underflows and reverts, bricking all reads of that LSD token.
hypotheses.attackPath: An untrusted actor cannot directly set the timestamp, but if the underlying API3 data feed ever publishes a future timestamp (which is possible with some oracle setups), every call to `getPrice_e36` for that token reverts. Any position using that token as collateral or debt becomes unliquidatable and unmanageable.
hypotheses.impact: Frozen funds / DoS on positions and liquidations that depend on the LSD oracle.
hypotheses.recommendation: Mirror the Api3OracleReader pattern: `if (block.timestamp > timestamp) { _require(block.timestamp - timestamp <= maxStaleTime, ...); }`.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.fillOrder uses stale order.collAmt vs current collateral
hypotheses.description: `_calculateFillOrderInfo` uses `_order.collAmt` (the amount recorded at order creation/update) to compute `collTokenAmt` via `toAmtCurrent`, but the position's actual collateral may have changed (e.g., via `removeCollateral` or `addCollateral`) since the order was created. `_calculateRepaySize` clamps `_order.collAmt` to `totalCollAmt`, but `_calculateFillOrderInfo` uses the unclamped `_order.collAmt` for `collTokenAmt`, so `amtOut` can exceed what the position actually holds.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner creates an order with `collAmt = X`, then removes collateral so the position holds less than X. A filler calls `fillOrder`; `_calculateFillOrderInfo` computes `amtOut` based on X, but `decollateralize` only transfers the actual (smaller) collateral to the filler, while the filler already paid `repayAmt` and `amtOut` to the recipient.
hypotheses.impact: Filler overpays; the order owner extracts value from fillers by shrinking collateral after order creation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Clamp `_order.collAmt` to the current `totalCollAmt` inside `_calculateFillOrderInfo` (or pass the clamped value from `_calculateRepaySize`).

hypotheses.title: InitCore.multicall health check runs after all delegatecalls, allowing mid-flight unhealthy states
hypotheses.description: InitCore.multicall sets isMulticallTx = true, executes all delegatecalls, and only then iterates uncheckedPosIds to verify health. During the multicall, any external call (e.g., token transfer in borrow/repay, or a callback into a hook) can observe or act on a position that is temporarily unhealthy. Because ensurePositionHealth only defers the check when isMulticallTx is true, an attacker who can trigger a callback mid-multicall (e.g., via a malicious token or a hook) can read the unhealthy state and act on it (e.g., liquidate or withdraw) before the final check reverts.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker crafts a multicall that borrows against collateral, then triggers an external call (token transfer to a malicious token) before depositing collateral. 2) During that external call, the attacker reenters InitCore.liquidate or a hook function that reads the position's health. 3) The position appears unhealthy (collateral not yet deposited), so the attacker liquidates it or extracts value. 4) The outer multicall's final health check may then revert, but the attacker's reentrant action already succeeded.
hypotheses.impact: Positions can be liquidated or manipulated based on transient unhealthy states within a multicall, causing loss of funds to position owners.
hypotheses.recommendation: Perform health checks incrementally or use a reentrancy guard that prevents external calls from observing mid-multicall state; alternatively, snapshot and restore health-relevant state around external calls.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder reverts on zero repayAmt, blocking order fills
hypotheses.description: In `fillOrder`, `_calculateFillOrderInfo` computes `repayAmt` from `_calculateRepaySize`. If the position's debt shares are zero (e.g., debt fully repaid via `repayDebt` or `reducePos`), `repayShares` and `repayAmt` become 0. The subsequent `IERC20(borrToken).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), repayAmt)` with 0 is fine, but `IInitCore(CORE).repay(marginPos.borrPool, repayShares, order.initPosId)` calls `_repay` which computes `amtToRepay = 0` and then `IERC20(tokenToRepay).safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, _pool, 0)` — this is fine, but `ILendingPool(_pool).repay(0)` calls `accrue` then `_shares.mulDiv(...)` with 0 shares; however `LendingPool.repay` requires `amt <= balance - cash` which holds for 0. The real issue: `_calculateRepaySize` divides by `totalCollAmt`; if `totalCollAmt == 0` (position collateral fully removed), division by zero reverts. `fillOrder` checks `getCollAmt == 0` and cancels, but a race where collateral is partially removed to a tiny amount combined with rounding can make `repayShares = 0` and `repayAmt = 0`, then `IInitCore.repay` with 0 shares reverts in `LendingPool.repay` because `_shares.mulDiv(_totalDebt, _totalDebtShares)` is 0 and `0 <= balance - cash` passes, but `totalDebtShares - 0` is fine. Actually the concrete DoS: `_calculateRepaySize` uses `totalCollAmt` from `getCollAmt`; if a user's order has `collAmt` set but the position's collateral was reduced below `collAmt`, `_order.collAmt` is clamped, but if `totalCollAmt` becomes 0 between the check and the call (reentrancy not possible here), it reverts. More reliably: `fillOrder` does not check `repayAmt != 0`; if `repayAmt == 0`, `IInitCore.repay` with `_shares == 0` will revert in `LendingPool.repay` because `_shares.mulDiv(_totalDebt, _totalDebtShares, Rounding.Up)` returns 0 and `0 <= balance - cash` is true, but `totalDebtShares = _totalDebtShares - 0` is fine — so no revert. The actual DoS is that `fillOrder` transfers `amtOut` of `order.tokenOut` from `msg.sender` to `order.recipient` BEFORE repaying; if `repayAmt` is 0 but `amtOut > 0`, the filler pays `amtOut` and gets nothing back because `decollateralize` with `order.collAmt` may revert if `order.collAmt > getCollAmt`. This is a griefing vector where an order can be made unfillable.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker creates a position and an order with `collAmt` equal to current collateral. 2. Attacker calls `reducePos` or `removeCollateral` to reduce collateral below `order.collAmt` (allowed since order is not checked against collateral on reduction). 3. Now `fillOrder` will clamp `_order.collAmt` to `totalCollAmt` in `_calculateRepaySize`, but `decollateralize` is called with the original `order.collAmt` (not the clamped value) in `fillOrder` — wait, `fillOrder` uses `order.collAmt` directly in `decollateralize`, which will revert if `order.collAmt > getCollAmt`. So the order becomes permanently unfillable until cancelled by owner.
hypotheses.impact: Orders become unfillable (DoS on fillOrder), but owner can cancel. Low impact.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `fillOrder`, clamp `order.collAmt` to current collateral before calling `decollateralize`, or check `order.collAmt <= getCollAmt` and cancel if not.

hypotheses.title: MoeSwapHelper accepts arbitrary deadline and path from untrusted caller
hypotheses.description: The swap helper decodes `(path, deadline)` directly from `_swapInfo.data` which is supplied by the caller of `MarginTradingHook` (via `_data`). There is no validation that `path[0] == tokenIn` and `path[last] == tokenOut`, nor that `deadline` is bounded. A malicious caller can pass an arbitrary path so the router swaps into an unrelated token, and the hook's `coreCallback` only checks the balance of `swapInfo.tokenOut` afterwards — but the helper transfers the swapped output back to the hook, so the hook's subsequent `safeTransfer` of `tokenOut` to the pool will revert or mis-account. More importantly, the deadline is fully attacker-controlled, allowing a swap to be held and executed at an arbitrary future time (or with `deadline = 0` reverting), enabling MEV/sandwich timing attacks against the position owner's collateral.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `MarginTradingHook.openPos`/`reducePos` with `_data` encoding a path that routes through an attacker-controlled pool or a stale deadline. 2) `MoeSwapHelper.swap` forwards the unvalidated path/deadline to the router. 3) Router executes the swap at attacker-favorable rates or reverts, and the hook's slippage check (`amtOut >= minAmtOut`) is the only guard, which the attacker can set to 0.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of position collateral via unfavorable swaps; potential griefing/DoS of legitimate positions by forcing reverts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `path[0] == _swapInfo.tokenIn` and `path[path.length-1] == _swapInfo.tokenOut`, and require `deadline >= block.timestamp` with a bounded max.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.cancelOrder lacks owner check on order
hypotheses.description: `cancelOrder` only checks `order.initPosId == initPosId` where `initPosId = initPosIds[msg.sender][_posId]`. It does not verify that `msg.sender` is the order's `recipient` or the position owner. Any address that can map a `_posId` to the same `initPosId` (e.g., via a shared/transferred position, or by front-running `initPosIds` mapping) can cancel another user's active order. Since `initPosIds` is keyed by `msg.sender`, an attacker who obtains the position NFT (or is authorized) can cancel orders they did not create.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker acquires authorization over a position (e.g., via `setApprovalForAll` or ownership transfer). 2) Attacker calls `cancelOrder` with the victim's `_orderId`. 3) Order is cancelled, denying the victim's stop-loss/take-profit protection.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service on risk-management orders; victim's position may be liquidated without the intended stop-loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == order.recipient` (or the position owner) in `cancelOrder`.

hypotheses.title: _calculateRepaySize uses stale totalCollAmt causing wrong repayShares
hypotheses.category: Off-by-one / stale state in order fill
hypotheses.description: `_calculateRepaySize` reads `totalCollAmt = getCollAmt(order.initPosId, collPool)` and `totalDebtShares = getPosDebtShares(...)`, then computes `repayShares = totalDebtShares * order.collAmt / totalCollAmt`. If `order.collAmt > totalCollAmt`, it clamps `order.collAmt = totalCollAmt`. However, `_calculateFillOrderInfo` then uses the clamped `order.collAmt` to compute `collTokenAmt = toAmtCurrent(order.collAmt)`, but `repayAmt` was computed from `repayShares` which used the clamped value. The issue is that `toAmtCurrent` accrues interest and can change `collTokenAmt` between the two calls, and more importantly, `_calculateFillOrderInfo` is called with the original `order` (memory copy) in `fillOrder`, so the clamping inside `_calculateRepaySize` does not propagate back to `_calculateFillOrderInfo`'s `order.collAmt`. This means `collTokenAmt` is computed from the unclamped `order.collAmt`, while `repayAmt` is computed from the clamped value — leading to `amtOut` being larger than the position can support.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker creates an order with `collAmt` larger than the position's actual collateral. 2) When `fillOrder` is called, `_calculateRepaySize` clamps `order.collAmt` to `totalCollAmt` for `repayShares`, but `_calculateFillOrderInfo` uses the original (larger) `order.collAmt` for `collTokenAmt`. 3) `amtOut` is computed as if the position had more collateral than it does. 4) The executor transfers `amtOut` to `order.recipient` and `repayAmt` to the hook, but `decollateralize` only removes the actual collateral, leaving the hook short.
hypotheses.impact: Executor overpays `amtOut` relative to the collateral actually removed; the hook may end up with a deficit or the tx reverts after partial transfers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Clamp `order.collAmt` once in `fillOrder` before calling both `_calculateRepaySize` and `_calculateFillOrderInfo`, or have `_calculateRepaySize` return the clamped value.

hypotheses.title: WLpMoeMasterChef reward accounting double-counts on wrap/unwrap
hypotheses.description: `unwrap` calls `_withdrawFromMasterChef` (which triggers `updateRewards`) and then `_transferRewards(_id, lpBalance, _to)` using the pre-withdraw `lpBalance`. `_transferRewards` computes `amt = (pidAccRewardPerShares - idAccRewardPerShares) * _amt / 1e18` and updates `idAccRewardPerShares` to the current pid value. Because `_withdrawFromMasterChef` already updated `pidAccRewardPerShares` for the remaining LP supply (which excludes the withdrawn amount), the reward delta is applied to the full pre-withdraw `lpBalance`, over-crediting the user relative to the LP actually deposited during the accrual period.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker wraps a large LP amount, waits for rewards to accrue. 2) Attacker calls `unwrap` for the full amount. 3) `updateRewards` accrues rewards based on the full LP supply (including attacker's), then `_transferRewards` pays the attacker based on the full `lpBalance` even though the LP was just withdrawn. 4) Attacker receives rewards proportional to LP that was not present for the entire accrual window, draining rewards from other LPs.
hypotheses.impact: Reward tokens are over-distributed to the attacker; other LPs receive less than their fair share; reward pool can be drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `unwrap`, call `_transferRewards` with the post-withdraw `lpBalance` (or update `idAccRewardPerShares` before withdrawing) so rewards are proportional to LP held during accrual.

hypotheses.title: coreCallback trusts swapHelper to return correct tokenOut amount
hypotheses.description: `coreCallback` transfers the entire `tokenIn` balance to `swapHelper` and then reads `IERC20(swapInfo.tokenOut).balanceOf(address(this))` to determine `amtOut`. For `CloseExactOut`, it asserts `balanceOf(tokenOut) == swapInfo.amtOut`, but for `OpenExactIn` and `CloseExactIn` there is no check that the swap actually produced a reasonable amount. A malicious or buggy `swapHelper` (set by governor, but the helper itself is an external contract that could be a router with unexpected behavior) can return far less than expected, and the hook will still transfer whatever it received to the pool. More critically, the hook does not verify that `swapHelper` actually spent the `tokenIn` — if the helper returns the tokens (e.g. via `_refund` in `MoeSwapHelper`), the hook's `tokenIn` balance is restored and the subsequent `balanceOf(tokenOut)` may be zero, silently depositing nothing.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys a malicious `swapHelper` (only possible if governor is compromised — excluded) OR exploits a legitimate helper's refund path: `MoeSwapHelper.swap` calls `_refund(_swapInfo.tokenIn)` which sends leftover `tokenIn` back to the hook. 2) If the router partially fills, the hook receives back `tokenIn` and less `tokenOut`; the hook then transfers the reduced `tokenOut` to the pool, minting fewer shares than expected. 3) In `_increasePosInternal`, the health check `_validateHealth` may still pass if the position was over-collateralized, but the user receives less collateral than intended.
hypotheses.impact: Users receive less collateral than expected; position health can be silently degraded; in extreme cases the position can be opened with near-zero collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `coreCallback`, after the swap, verify `amtOut >= minAmtOut` (passed via `SwapInfo`) and that `tokenIn` balance is zero (or account for refunds explicitly).

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.fillOrder lets filler choose repayShares via collAmt scaling, mispricing repay
hypotheses.description: `_calculateRepaySize` scales `repayShares = totalDebtShares * _order.collAmt / totalCollAmt` and then `repayAmt = debtShareToAmtCurrent(repayShares)`. The order owner sets `_order.collAmt` at creation, but the position's `totalCollAmt` and `totalDebtShares` change over time (interest accrual, other orders, addCollateral). A filler can call `fillOrder` when the ratio has drifted so that the computed `repayAmt` is smaller than the value of collateral actually decollateralized (`order.collAmt`), letting the filler take collateral worth more than the debt repaid.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes an active order. 2) Attacker manipulates position state (e.g. via addCollateral/repayDebt on their own position, or waits for interest accrual) so that `totalDebtShares * order.collAmt / totalCollAmt` yields a small `repayAmt`. 3) Attacker calls `fillOrder`, pays the small `repayAmt`, and receives `order.collAmt` of collateral. 4) Attacker profits the difference; order owner's position loses collateral without proportional debt reduction.
hypotheses.impact: Order owner loses collateral; debt remains disproportionately high; position can become unhealthy and liquidatable.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute `repayAmt` from the current debt-to-collateral ratio at fill time using the same snapshot, or require `repayAmt` to be at least the pro-rata debt for `order.collAmt` at fill time.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.removeCollateral transfers entire contract balance, not just redeemed amount
hypotheses.description: `removeCollateral` calls `burnTo(marginPos.collPool, address(this))` and then transfers `IERC20(collToken).balanceOf(address(this))` — the entire contract balance — to the caller. If any collToken was already sitting in the hook (e.g. from a prior partial operation, a donation, or a concurrent multicall), it is swept out along with the redeemed amount. This lets a caller drain stray tokens that belong to other users or pending operations.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes or induces stray collToken balance in the hook (e.g. via a failed/partial multicall, or by donating). 2) Attacker calls `removeCollateral` with a small `_shares`. 3) The hook redeems a small amount but transfers the full balance, including the stray tokens, to the attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of stray tokens; loss of funds for other users whose tokens were temporarily held by the hook.
hypotheses.recommendation: Capture the balance before `burnTo` and transfer only the delta, or transfer the exact redeemed amount returned by `burnTo`.

hypotheses.title: MoneyMarketHook.execute lacks reentrancy guard on helper callbacks
hypotheses.description: execute() is nonReentrant, but it calls IRebaseHelper(helper).wrap/unwrap and IInitCore(CORE).multicall, which in turn call back into the hook via ERC721HolderUpgradeable and token transfers. The whitelisted helper is trusted, but the underlying rebase token (e.g., mUSD) can have hooks. More importantly, execute() reads initPosIds[msg.sender][posId] and checks ownerOf before the multicall, but the multicall can change position ownership or state mid-flight; the final health check uses the same initPosId without re-validating ownership.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls execute with a posId they own. 2) During the multicall, a token callback (e.g., from a rebase token) reenters execute with a different posId that the attacker also controls. 3) The reentrant call operates on a position whose state is mid-update, potentially bypassing the intended ordering of repay/withdraw/borrow/deposit.
hypotheses.impact: State inconsistencies in position accounting; potential to borrow against collateral that is being withdrawn in the outer call, leading to unhealthy positions.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a reentrancy guard to createPos and any function callable during the multicall, and re-validate ownership/health after all external calls.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.fillOrder has no deadline and no partial-fill protection
hypotheses.description: `fillOrder` executes an active order with no deadline, no nonce, and no signature. Any external actor can call it at any time as long as the trigger price condition holds. Because the order's `recipient` is fixed at creation and the executor supplies `borrToken` and receives `collAmt` collateral, an attacker can wait for the most favorable price movement (within the trigger band) and fill the order, extracting value from the position owner. There is no `deadline` field in `Order`, so an order created long ago can be filled at a stale but still-triggering price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner creates a stop-loss/take-profit order. 2) Attacker monitors the oracle; when the mark price is at the edge of the trigger band (most favorable to attacker), calls `fillOrder`. 3) Attacker receives `order.collAmt` collateral and pays `repayAmt` borrow tokens, pocketing the difference.
hypotheses.impact: Position owner receives less than intended; attacker extracts value from the position's collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a `deadline` field to `Order` and require `block.timestamp <= deadline` in `fillOrder`; also consider a signed order or restricting fill to the owner.

hypotheses.title: MoneyMarketHook.execute lacks nonce/deadline; repay uses msg.value for multiple ops
hypotheses.description: `execute` processes `_params` with no nonce or deadline, and `_handleRepay` uses `msg.value` for every WNATIVE repay entry in the loop. If multiple repay params reference WNATIVE, the first iteration consumes `msg.value` via `IWNative.deposit{value: msg.value}()`, and subsequent iterations will attempt to deposit the same `msg.value` again (which reverts or double-counts). More critically, the lack of a deadline means a signed/relayed `execute` payload (if used via meta-transaction) can be replayed. Even without signatures, the `msg.value` reuse across loop iterations is a concrete accounting bug.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker (or victim) submits `execute` with two WNATIVE repay params and `msg.value = X`. 2) First iteration deposits X and repays. 3) Second iteration attempts to deposit X again, but the contract's balance is now 0, causing a revert or, if the contract holds extra WNATIVE, draining it.
hypotheses.impact: Revert/DoS of legitimate multi-repay operations; potential drain of pre-existing WNATIVE balance in the hook.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track remaining `msg.value` across loop iterations and only deposit the unused portion; add a deadline parameter.

hypotheses.title: _transmitTokenIn mishandles msg.value when tokenIn is not WNATIVE
hypotheses.category: Wrong assumption about msg.value / token accounting
hypotheses.description: `_transmitTokenIn` only checks `_tokenIn == WNATIVE` when `msg.value != 0`. If a user calls `openPos`/`increasePos`/`addCollateral`/`repayDebt` with `msg.value > 0` but `_tokenIn` is a non-WNATIVE token, the modifier `depositNative` wraps the ETH into WNATIVE and the function proceeds to `safeTransferFrom` the full `_amt` of the non-native token. The wrapped WNATIVE stays in the contract and is later refunded by `refundNative` — but the user has effectively paid both `msg.value` (refunded) and `_amt` of the ERC20. This is not a direct loss, but the `depositNative` modifier wraps ETH that is never used, and `refundNative` unwraps and returns it. The real issue is that `_transmitTokenIn` does not revert when `msg.value != 0 && _tokenIn != WNATIVE` in all paths — it does `_require(_tokenIn == WNATIVE, ...)` only inside the `if (msg.value != 0)` block, which is correct, but the check happens after `depositNative` already wrapped the ETH. If the require fails, the whole tx reverts, so no loss. However, in `MoneyMarketHook._handleRepay`, the same pattern is used without the `_require`, and `msg.value` is consumed by `IWNative.deposit` even when `uToken != WNATIVE`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `MoneyMarketHook.execute` with `msg.value > 0` and a `repayParams` entry whose pool's underlying token is not WNATIVE. 2) `_handleRepay` sees `uToken != WNATIVE`, so it does not deposit `msg.value`; but the `msg.value` is still held by the hook. 3) If `_params.returnNative` is false, the ETH is stuck in the hook (no refund path). 4) Attacker can repeat to accumulate ETH in the hook, or another user's tx can sweep it via `returnNative`.
hypotheses.impact: ETH can be permanently stuck in `MoneyMarketHook` when `msg.value > 0` but no WNATIVE operation consumes it and `returnNative` is false.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `MoneyMarketHook.execute`, require `msg.value == 0` unless at least one operation uses WNATIVE, or always refund unused ETH regardless of `returnNative`.

hypotheses.title: LendingPool.repay uses balanceOf check that can be bypassed via direct transfer
hypotheses.description: `repay` computes `amt = _shares.mulDiv(_totalDebt, _totalDebtShares, Rounding.Up)` and requires `amt <= IERC20(underlyingToken).balanceOf(address(this)) - _cash`. This check assumes that any tokens transferred to the pool since the last `cash` update are repayments. However, `cash` is only updated in `mint`, `burn`, `borrow`, `repay`, and `accrueInterest`. If someone directly transfers underlying tokens to the pool (donation), `balanceOf - cash` is inflated, allowing `repay` to succeed even if the caller did not transfer the tokens. More importantly, `InitCore._repay` transfers tokens from `msg.sender` to the pool *before* calling `ILendingPool.repay`, so the check passes. But if `_shares` is larger than the position's debt, `InitCore` clamps it, so this is not directly exploitable. The real issue is that `cash` is not updated on direct transfers, so `totalAssets()` under-reports and share price is wrong.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker donates underlying tokens directly to the pool. 2) `cash` is not updated, so `totalAssets()` is lower than actual balance. 3) `toShares`/`toAmt` use stale `totalAssets`, allowing attacker to mint more shares than fair value (or redeem more). 4) Attacker can also use the inflated `balanceOf - cash` to repay debt without transferring tokens.
hypotheses.impact: Share price manipulation; attacker can mint shares at a discount or repay debt with the pool's own donated tokens.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update `cash` on every state-changing function by reading `balanceOf` at the start, or use an internal accounting variable that is only updated via `mint`/`burn`/`borrow`/`repay`.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.fillOrder transfers amtOut before verifying repayment succeeds
hypotheses.description: In `fillOrder`, the contract first pulls `repayAmt` of borrToken from the filler, then transfers `amtOut` of `order.tokenOut` to `order.recipient`, and only afterwards calls `IInitCore(CORE).repay(...)` and `decollateralize(...)`. If `repay` reverts (e.g. due to paused pool, cap, or rounding), the whole tx reverts, so no direct loss — but if `decollateralize` reverts after repay succeeded, the filler has paid debt and received nothing while the position's debt was reduced. More importantly, `amtOut` is computed from `_calculateFillOrderInfo` using `toAmtCurrent` which accrues interest, but `repayAmt` is computed separately; a mismatch between the two accrual snapshots can leave the position with residual debt or over-repaid debt.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `fillOrder` at a block where interest accrual between `_calculateFillOrderInfo` and `repay` changes `debtShareToAmtCurrent`. 2) `repayAmt` paid by filler differs from the debt actually cleared, leaving dust debt or overpayment. 3) Attacker repeats to extract value from rounding drift.
hypotheses.impact: Dust debt accumulation; position health drift; potential over/under payment to filler.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot debt conversion once and reuse; perform repay before transferring `amtOut`, or use a single accrual snapshot for both calculations.

hypotheses.title: fillOrder transfers amtOut before repay, allowing filler to lose funds on repay failure
hypotheses.description: In `fillOrder`, the sequence is: (1) transfer `repayAmt` of `borrToken` from `msg.sender` to hook, (2) transfer `amtOut` of `order.tokenOut` from `msg.sender` to `order.recipient`, (3) repay, (4) decollateralize to `msg.sender`. If step (3) or (4) reverts (e.g., because `order.collAmt > getCollAmt` due to prior collateral reduction, or because `repay` fails due to paused pool), the entire tx reverts, so the filler's funds are returned. However, if `order.tokenOut == borrToken`, then step (2) transfers `amtOut` of `borrToken` from filler to recipient, and step (1) already transferred `repayAmt` of `borrToken` from filler. The filler pays `repayAmt + amtOut` but only receives `order.collAmt` of collateral. If `amtOut` is large, the filler may overpay. This is a design issue but not a DoS.
hypotheses.attackPath: Filler miscalculates and overpays.
hypotheses.impact: Filler loses funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reorder to decollateralize before transferring amtOut, or compute net amounts.

hypotheses.title: LendingPool.repay allows repaying more than position debt, minting free cash
hypotheses.description: `LendingPool.repay` computes `amt = _shares.mulDiv(_totalDebt, _totalDebtShares, Rounding.Up)` and requires `amt <= balanceOf(this) - cash`. It does not cap `_shares` to `totalDebtShares`. If `_shares > totalDebtShares`, `totalDebtShares = _totalDebtShares - _shares` underflows and reverts, so that path is safe. However, `InitCore._repay` caps `sharesToRepay` to `positionDebtShares`, but `LendingPool.repay` is also callable via `InitCore.repay` with `_shares` capped only to position debt. The pool's `totalDebtShares` may be less than the sum of position debt shares if accounting drifts (e.g. via `updatePosDebtShares` rounding), allowing a position to repay shares that exceed its fair share of pool debt, inflating `cash` and diluting other lenders.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker opens a position, borrows, then exploits rounding in `updatePosDebtShares` to accumulate debt shares slightly above the pool's `totalDebtShares` proportion. 2) Attacker repays the position's full debt shares; `LendingPool.repay` credits `cash` with `amt` computed from pool totals, which may exceed the actual debt attributable to the position. 3) Attacker's position is debt-free while the pool's `totalDebt` is reduced by less than the cash added, leaving a surplus that dilutes other lenders.
hypotheses.impact: Lenders' share value is diluted; pool accounting drifts; potential insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `LendingPool.repay`, require `_shares <= totalDebtShares` and cap `amt` to the actual debt reduction.

hypotheses.title: MarginTradingHook.removeCollateral has no health check after withdrawal
hypotheses.description: `removeCollateral` calls `IInitCore.decollateralize` which enforces `ensurePositionHealth`, but the hook then calls `burnTo` and transfers the underlying out. The `decollateralize` health check uses the position's health at that moment; however, `burnTo` redeems pool shares at the current exchange rate, and the hook transfers the entire `collToken` balance of the contract to the user. If the pool's share price changed between `decollateralize` and `burnTo` (or if the hook holds pre-existing collToken balance from another operation), the user can withdraw more underlying than the collateral removed, leaving the position under-collateralized.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deposits collateral via `addCollateral` (hook holds collToken briefly). 2) Attacker calls `removeCollateral` with `_shares` such that `decollateralize` passes health check. 3) `burnTo` redeems shares; if the hook's collToken balance includes dust from prior operations, the attacker receives more than the redeemed amount. 4) Position health is now below 1e18 but no post-transfer check is performed.
hypotheses.impact: Position becomes under-collateralized; protocol accrues bad debt.
hypotheses.recommendation: After `burnTo`, re-validate position health via `_validateHealth` and transfer only the amount corresponding to the burned shares.

hypotheses.title: removeCollateralWLpTo can be griefed by front-running harvest with zero rewards
hypotheses.description: `removeCollateralWLpTo` calls `_harvest` which calls `IBaseWrapLp(_wLp).harvest(_tokenId, address(this))`. In `WLpMoeMasterChef.harvest`, `_claimFromMasterChef` is called which triggers `updateRewards` modifier. If the masterchef's `claim` reverts (e.g., due to a paused or broken rewarder), the entire `removeCollateralWLpTo` reverts, blocking decollateralization and thus blocking withdrawals/liquidations. An attacker cannot directly cause this, but if the external masterchef is paused or a reward token is blacklisted, funds are stuck.
hypotheses.attackPath: External dependency failure, not attacker-controlled.
hypotheses.impact: Stuck funds if masterchef fails.
hypotheses.recommendation: Wrap harvest in try/catch or make it optional.

hypotheses.title: LendingPool.burn reverts if sharesToBurn is zero, blocking empty withdrawals
hypotheses.description: `burn` requires `sharesToBurn != 0`. If a user calls `removeCollateral` with `_shares == 0`, `decollateralize` calls `removeCollateralTo` which requires `_shares > 0`, so it reverts earlier. But if `decollateralize` is called with a small amount that rounds to 0 shares in the pool, `burn` reverts. This can block withdrawals of dust amounts.
hypotheses.attackPath: User tries to withdraw dust, tx reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Dust stuck.
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow zero-share burn or handle dust.
